decisions.statement: A git write is refused unless the line proves the call cannot reach akasha.
A git write in the command word is refused unless the line gives that proof.
A flag that writes nothing is that proof.
A `-C` path resolving to another repository is that proof.
Nothing else on a line is that proof.
A refusal names the akasha command that does the git write asked for with its flags filled in.
An akasha command stands aside here and commits for itself.
A prefix that only runs the call behind that prefix does not hide a git write from this hook.
No pathspec on the line lets a git write through.
A refusal prescribes no bounded form of the call that refusal refused.
`rm` is not named here.
`checkout` is not named here.
`restore` is not named here.
`block-destructive-git` names `rm`.
`block-destructive-git` names `checkout`.
`block-destructive-git` names `restore`.
An act left to `block-destructive-git` is refused in every form the act is written in.
Every path the akasha repository tracks is akasha content.
The akasha repository is checked out outside the akasha folder as well as inside it.
Two checkouts sharing one git folder are one repository under two toplevels.
Where a call runs is on the line only where `-C` puts it there.
A `-C` path is resolved through its symlinks before a repository is read from it.
Several `-C` on one line accumulate, each against the one before it.
A `-C` path that resolves to no other repository is refused.
A relative `-C` path proves nothing, because the cwd is not on the line.
A line carrying a global flag before the act other than `-C` proves nothing.
The paths a commit would carry are in the index rather than on the command line.
A shell writes a file in more ways than can be named.
This hook reads git alone.
A hand-written commit does not leave the index stamp behind HEAD.
A read flag is read as a flag rather than as another flag's value.

definition: a refusal of the git calls that write tracked akasha content outside the commands
